subject: 💸 AI fortunes in flux

Plus: Sentiment check | Friday, November 20, 2026

Axios Macro
By Courtenay Brown and Neil Irwin · Nov 20, 2026

📉 What the stock market giveth, the stock market taketh away. The AI boom's wealth surge could cut both ways for the overall economy. More below.

  • Plus, the first post-election read on consumer sentiment.

Today's newsletter, edited by George Moriarty and copy edited by Katie Lewis, is 778 words, a 3-minute read.
 
 
1 big thing: AI wealth's ripple effects
 

Illustration: Natalie Peeples/Axios
 

The AI boom is generating enormous fortunes, from stock-market gains (that are now under pressure) to the paper wealth being amassed as AI firms go public.

Why it matters: Changes in household wealth can ripple through the economy, influencing everything from housing prices in tech hubs to consumer spending nationally, even before much of that wealth is converted into cash.

  • But the stock market's recent sell-off underscores how the wealth effect cuts both ways — supporting spending as asset prices rise and weighing on it if the AI boom dramatically reverses.

The big picture: AI is already helping power economic growth through massive investment in data centers, chips and other infrastructure.

  • AI-related investment contributed an estimated 0.47 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth over the year through mid-2026, roughly one-fifth of the increase, according to JPMorgan.
  • AI-driven stock market gains are also boosting spending. Federal Reserve vice chair Philip Jefferson said last week: "That added wealth appears to be raising household spending."

What they're saying: Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told reporters yesterday that the AI boom's massive investment spending has so far posed a greater risk of overheating the economy than the spending of newly wealthy shareholders.

  • "Look, a $1.5 trillion IPO — the question of what are people going to do with the money that they now have some access to, that liquidity is going to become a macro-relevant statistic," Goolsbee said, referring to Anthropic's public market debut.
  • "We're watching that more than fearing that it's already been in effect," he added.

Yes, but: The recent sell-off threatens to erode some of the wealth created during the AI rally.

  • The S&P 500 is about 10% below its recent peak, while the Nasdaq is down nearly 16% below its record high.
  • Anthropic shares surged at the start of Thursday's debut before giving up much of those gains. The stock is down as much as 11% this morning.

What to watch: Much of the wealth held by employees and early investors at private AI firms remains difficult to access. Lockup periods, taxes and decisions about selling will determine how much becomes available to spend.

  • Even before that wealth becomes liquid, it may already be reshaping local economies, particularly San Francisco's red-hot luxury housing market.
  • In the first half of 2026, 144 homes sold for at least $1 million above asking price, compared with just eight homes a year earlier, according to Compass.

The effects may be most pronounced in markets where wealthy tech workers are competing for a limited supply of desirable goods.

  • In other words, it could drive up prices in certain markets without necessarily producing a meaningful increase in nationwide consumer spending or inflation.

The bottom line: Bank of America economists this month called a sustained AI-driven stock market correction "one of the larger risks to the US and global economy," warning it could weaken both investment and consumer spending.

2. Post-midterms sentiment surge
 
Data: University of Michigan; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios

Consumer sentiment has popped this month, amid midterm elections and a moderation in energy prices.

The big picture: Sentiment remains below its pre-Iran War levels, but Americans felt better about their personal finances this month — and view the soon-to-be divided government as better for their pocketbooks.

  • Expectations surged for independents and Democrats but fell for Republicans, which supports the idea that sentiment was influenced by respondents' view of the midterm election results.

By the numbers: The University of Michigan's overall consumer sentiment index was 51.5 in November, up from 48 in October. That 7.3% rise was fueled by a particularly strong gain in expectations for the future (up 8.4%).

  • Median expectations for inflation over the next year plunged to 4.7% from 3.7% in October, and longer-run inflation expectations dropped as well, to 3.3% from 3.5%.

What they're saying: "Consumers appear to anticipate potential changes to public policy under a divided government to come," wrote survey director Joanne Hsu.

  • Meanwhile, personal financial conditions improved for low-wealth and middle-wealth consumers, the latter of which "experienced some relief" with gas prices falling.
  • "In contrast, those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances, consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets," Hsu notes.

Reality check: Sentiment remains 9% below its February level, before the Iran conflict, and consumers' inflation expectations remain above their 2024 range.

  • Hsu wrote that "consumers continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation — rather than unemployment — will cause greater hardship" in the next year or two.
